# The *Co-Operating* Model.

I'm sitting across from a CEO looking at her P&L and her headcount report side by side. Good company. Profitable. Growing. She bought AI software fourteen months ago — a meaningful line on the books. She ran a rollout. Her team is using the tools. And I'm scrolling across the two reports and I see the thing I keep seeing: the headcount line and the revenue line are moving together, exactly the way they were before the software. Same slope. Same ratio. Quarter after quarter. The AI subscription is right there, third line down — and it has changed nothing structural.

She has done everything right. She identified the problem, bought a credible solution, and deployed it. And the headcount curve didn't bend.

I've seen this enough times to know what it is. She dropped a highly capable synthetic worker into an organization designed exclusively for humans. Think about that as a hiring scenario: if you brought on a new employee but gave them no seat on the org chart, no defined handoffs, and no accountability for any outcome, that employee's work would die in the gap. Every piece of output they produced would dissolve somewhere between their desk and the person who needed it. The AI is failing for the exact same reason. Not because the tool doesn't work. Because the business wasn't designed for a non-human worker.

That is an operating design failure. And the Co-Operating Model is the answer to it.

The diagnosis was the easy part. You have an operating-model problem, not a technology problem. The harder question — the one this chapter answers — is what the right operating model looks like. Not in the abstract, and not as a vision deck. As a structure you can draw on a whiteboard, point at, and start running against on Monday. That structure has a name in this book. We call it the Co-Operating Model. It is what a Co-Intelligent Company is built on, and it is what makes *Co-Intelligent Co-operation* — humans and AI working the same problems together — something other than an accident.

## What a *Co-Intelligent Company* is.

Three terms in that paragraph are doing specific work and they are easy to blur together. Here is what each one means.

The **Co-Intelligent Company** is the identity layer — what a company becomes when humans and AI work as one system, not two parallel tracks. Not a company that uses AI tools. Not a company that has an AI strategy. A company where the human and the synthetic are integrated into a single operating system, designed to run together from the start.

**Co-Intelligent Co-operation** is the relational frame — the activity of humans and AI working the same problems together, inside the same loop, against the same outcome. Not relegated to a sprint or a project — it is what the company does, continuously, as its default way of working.

The **Co-Operating Model** is the system frame — the structure that makes Co-Intelligent Co-operation possible. It is the explicit design of who brings what intelligence to the work and who owns which operating responsibility inside it.

The CEO in the opening story has a company that uses AI. She does not yet have a Co-Intelligent Company. The difference is not the tools she bought. It is the operating model she hasn't built yet.

## What *AI* actually is.

Most executives have met one kind of AI: a chat window. You type something, it responds. You close the tab. Nothing changes in the company. That experience is accurate as far as it goes — it just doesn't go very far.

A chatbot is an interface. You ask a question, you get an answer, the interaction ends. Input, output, done. Every tool you have used for the last thirty years works this way — a spreadsheet, a search engine, a CRM. You supply something and the system returns something. The loop does not continue unless you start it again.

An agent is different. An agent holds a goal, takes a sequence of steps toward it, evaluates its own output, and adjusts — without you re-prompting it between steps. It does not wait. It works. When I run an agent team on a content build, I am not typing questions and reading answers. I am managing a production process. I set the direction. The agents run the work. I review, redirect, and ship. The loop closes when the outcome is right, not when the timer runs out.

That distinction — chatbot as input/output tool, agent as iterative co-worker — is the one that matters for operating design. A chatbot gives you a productivity improvement localized to the person typing. An agent gives you a structural change, because the loop can run without the human inside every step.

The technology underneath both is the same: large language models, trained on text to recognize and generate language at scale. What separates a chatbot from an agent is not the model. It is the architecture around the model — how it is instructed, what tools it has access to, how it evaluates its own output, and how it hands work back to a human or to another agent.

One more concept matters for the operating model: organizational memory. Most AI tools, out of the box, have no memory of your company. They know the world; they do not know you. Embedding models and retrieval systems let you connect an AI to your own documents, your CRM, your transcripts, your SOPs. The result is a system that reasons against your actual context, not the general case.

I think of this as the organizational brain — the knowledge that used to live in people's heads, in files no one could find, in systems that didn't talk to each other — made accessible to the agents running the work. When the developer who had been with me for years put in his notice, the knowledge walked out with him. An organization with a well-built memory layer does not have that exposure. The knowledge stays because it was designed to stay. The agents can reach it on demand.

The humans in that system are not outside it. They are nodes — the ones who supply judgment, direction, and correction that no model can supply from training data alone. I work alongside my agents or manage agent teams, and together we iterate toward an outcome that is not predictable from the inputs the way a spreadsheet result is predictable. It is arrived at through cycles of generation, review, and adjustment. It is better for having gone through them.

That is what the Co-Operating Model is designed to support. Not AI as a tab you open when you feel like it. AI as a workforce you design, direct, and compound on.

## Two words, two *jobs*.

*Co-Intelligent Co-operation* is the activity. *Co-Operating Model* is the structure.

Co-Intelligent Co-operation is the relational frame. It names what humans and AI are doing when the thing is working — working the same problems together, in the same loop, against the same outcome. Not humans doing tasks while AI does tasks in some adjacent track. One system, one set of problems, two kinds of intelligence pointed at it. That is the activity.

The Co-Operating Model is the system frame. It is the structure that makes the activity possible — the explicit decisions, written down, about who brings what intelligence to the work and who owns which operating responsibility inside it. A company without a Co-Operating Model can still occasionally produce Co-Intelligent Co-operation — in the way a company without an org chart can still occasionally complete a project. It just can't do it on purpose, can't do it repeatedly, and can't compound on it. The model is what turns a lucky outcome into a designed one.

The reason most companies that have invested in AI have no compounding return is that they jumped to the activity without ever building the structure. They put a tool next to the existing workflow and asked the team to figure it out. The Co-Operating Model is the work they skipped.

## Why the *Co* is load-bearing.

The last decade of enterprise software pitched a graft — a productivity layer bolted on top of the existing org. The metaphor was addition. You had a worker; now the worker has a tool. The shape of the work, the shape of the org, the shape of the accountabilities — none of that changes. You just expect more output from the same structure.

Co-Intelligence is different. The human and the agent are both inside the loop. The work itself gets re-shaped around the fact that two kinds of intelligence are now executing it. The structure is built to evolve — because the agent gets smarter every quarter, the human's task space shifts as a result, and the design has to keep pace. The *Co* is what gives the company that joint mechanism for continually evolving. A graft produces a frozen artifact. Co-Intelligence produces a living system.

A graft treats AI the way the last generation of software treated every tool: input, output, done. Co-Intelligence treats the agent as an iterative co-worker inside an open-ended loop. The agent does not just return an answer. It works a problem through multiple cycles, hands its output to a human for judgment, takes the correction, and runs again. That loop is what makes the system learn. A graft cannot learn. It can only repeat.

It is the difference between a company that absorbs every model upgrade as a free improvement to its operating model, and a company that has to re-run a change-management project every time the technology takes a step.

I described in the preface the moment a key developer left my company — I paid for the ladder and absorbed the cost of the chute. That is what the graft model produces over time: frozen knowledge, frozen structure, and then a single departure that undoes years of investment. Co-Intelligence is the architecture that prevents it. The knowledge stays because it was designed to stay.

## What each one *brings*.

The agent is idle until someone tells it what to do. It has no curiosity. It has no agenda. It does not know what quarter you are in, what your biggest customer is threatening, or what "good" looks like for your company this year. It knows none of that until you transmit it.

That is not a bug. That is the architecture. And it is the architecture most companies get backwards.

Humans carry a world model. We build it constantly — from every conversation, every mistake, every relationship, every quarter we have lived inside the business. That model tells us what matters, what a decision costs, what a number means when it lands inside the context of everything else we know. We use it so automatically we forget it is there.

Agents do not have one. They have pattern recognition at a scale no human can match, and memory that does not degrade. But they have no ground truth about your situation. They have no felt sense of what is at stake. Left without direction, they will produce something — and it will be technically coherent and contextually wrong in ways that take real judgment to catch.

Think about the worst manager you ever had. The one who handed you a task with no background, no success criteria, no sense of what they actually needed or why it mattered. You did your best. The work landed badly. Nobody was happy. The failure was not yours — it was the manager's failure to transmit.

We do the same thing to agents. Constantly.

The human's job in the Co-Operating Model is not to be creative while the agent is analytical. That split is wrong and it produces badly designed workflows. The real split is simpler: the human is the transmitter of a world model and a desired outcome. The agent is the executor that can only work from what was transmitted.

Get that transmission right and the agent produces work that is hard to distinguish from what a skilled person would produce. Get it wrong — give the agent a task without context, a question without background, a deliverable without a definition of good — and you get the equivalent of that badly briefed employee. Technically busy. Contextually adrift.

<!-- DIAGRAM: Two-column visual contrast — Human intelligence (judgment, context, strategy/taste/ethics) vs. Agent intelligence (memory at scale, pattern recognition, tireless synthesis) — styled to make the split feel definitive, not hierarchical -->
<!-- FORMAT: table -->
<!-- PRIORITY: must-have -->

| The Human brings the intelligence of | The Agent brings the intelligence of |
|---|---|
| Judgment under ambiguity | Memory at scale |
| Context, history, relationships | Pattern recognition across your data |
| Strategy, taste, ethics | Tireless synthesis from broad sources |

The left column is the world model. The right column is what becomes possible once the world model has been transmitted.

Before you read the next section, pick one role in your company — yours, or a direct report's — and ask: what percentage of that person's week is spent on work that belongs in the right column? That number is your baseline.

## What each one *owns*.

Ownership is where most companies stall, and it is the only variable that determines whether the work compounds.

The way I use "ownership" here is specific. It does not mean who is aware of a task or who is cc'd on the outcome. It means who is accountable for the decision, the quality, and the next move if something goes wrong. One person — or one agent — per responsibility. Not shared. Not "we'll figure it out in the meeting." A single owner who picks up the work and does not put it down until the handoff is complete.

If you have worked inside Tiago Forte's PARA system — Projects, Areas, Resources, Archives — you already have a useful frame. Forte separates work into things with a finish line (Projects) and things that are ongoing (Areas), and makes the case that most knowledge-work gets lost because people treat ongoing responsibilities as if they were projects, and vice versa. The ownership split in the Co-Operating Model works the same way. Some responsibilities have a finish line: a draft gets written, an analysis gets delivered, a campaign gets published. Others are ongoing: the human owns the outcome across time, coaches the system as it learns, and is accountable if the work drifts. The table below maps both.

Here is what that looks like in practice before you see the table.

Compound runs a weekly content cycle. At the start of the week, our marketing lead decides what we are publishing — which topic, which angle, which channel. That decision is hers. Not the agent's. The agent does not know what conversation I had at a conference last Thursday, or what landed badly with the audience two weeks ago, or which piece of content our best clients have been forwarding to their own teams. She does.

Once she decides, the agent takes the brief and produces the first draft — copy, visual direction, distribution plan. She does not write the first sentence. She reads the output, marks what is right and what is wrong, and the agent revises. The draft never leaves her without her judgment on it. She owns the outcome. The agent owns the output that precedes it.

That distinction sounds small. It is not. When output and outcome get confused — when the agent is treated as the decision-maker, or the human is kept inside the execution — the whole loop collapses.

<!-- DIAGRAM: Two-column ownership table — Human (decide, direct, price, own, coach) vs. Agent (draft, recommend, document, monitor, execute) — verbs should be visually prominent; this is the structural heart of the chapter -->
<!-- FORMAT: table -->
<!-- PRIORITY: must-have -->

| The Human owns the operating responsibility of | The Agent owns the operating responsibility of |
|---|---|
| Deciding what's worth solving | Research, drafting, first-pass analysis |
| Directing the work; pricing the cost | Decision support and recommendations |
| Owning the outcome and the risk | Documentation, capture, monitoring |
| Coaching the system over time | Executing the routine, on call, on time |

The human side is almost entirely verbs of judgment and direction — *decides, directs, prices, owns, coaches*. The agent side is almost entirely verbs of execution and capture — *drafts, recommends, documents, monitors, executes*. The human is not in the workflow as a faster operator. The human is in the workflow as the operator of the operators. That is the shift that makes the math work.

The two columns are the load-bearing logic of the model. A company that lets agents start deciding what's worth solving has lost the plot — the agent does not know what business you are in, what your reputation is worth, or what a bad week feels like with your largest customer. A company that keeps the human inside the documentation and the first-pass drafting has wasted the model — that work has just moved sideways at high cost.

When you get the split right, the company compounds. The human's hours flow into the work only humans can do: deciding, directing, pricing, owning, coaching. The agent's hours flow into everything else, at a cost and speed that re-prices the underlying economics of the business. Both sides get compounding returns every quarter, because the structure was built to absorb improvement on both sides.

Look at the role you picked a moment ago. Map what that person actually does against the two columns — not what you'd like them to do, what they do today. The gap between their current task list and the left column is the redesign work the rest of this book will help you do.

When you get it wrong — and most companies get it wrong on first attempt — you get the failure mode we keep seeing in the field: two parallel tracks producing nothing structural. The team has its workflow. The agents have theirs. The handoff is undefined. The outcome belongs to no one. The dashboard shows tool adoption and the P&L shows nothing.

Here is what it looks like when you get it right.

Our marketing lead manages content and video production for Compound. Before we applied the model, that meant she was the doer — writing the copy, editing the video, building the assets, one task at a time. After, we stopped and looked at what was actually happening on her screen. Claude Design was working on the visual assets. Claude AI was drafting copy. NotebookLM was pulling and synthesizing source material. HeyGen was handling the video. Four agent teams. Four workstreams. All pointed at the same output. And she was not editing a video. She was not writing a caption. She was deciding whether the outputs were right. She was steering.

<!-- DIAGRAM: Before/after illustration — "Before": one person connected to a stack of tasks; "After": one person at the center directing four named agent workstreams (Claude Design, Claude AI, NotebookLM, HeyGen) all pointing at a single output -->
<!-- FORMAT: diagram -->
<!-- PRIORITY: must-have -->

Her job did not get smaller. It got higher.

That shift has a structural name: parallel workstreams. It is not optional in a well-designed Co-Operating Model.

Linear work has a shape everyone recognizes: finish this before starting that. Write the copy, then build the asset, then edit the video. One person, one task in queue, one output at a time. That shape made sense when all the workers were human — a person can only work one task at a time. The constraint was biological, so the operating model was built around it.

Agents do not have that constraint. Four agents can run simultaneously. The design agent, the copy agent, the research agent, the video agent — they do not wait on each other. The work that used to move in a line now moves in parallel, and the wall-clock time collapses.

That is what was happening on her screen. Claude Design, Claude AI, NotebookLM, and HeyGen were not running in sequence. They were running at once, each on its own workstream, all pointed at the same output. The production cycle that used to take a week did not get faster because any one tool was faster. It got faster because the four pieces of it were happening simultaneously.

The compounding math is direct. Parallelism reduces calendar time for every sprint. Reduced sprint time means more sprints per quarter. More sprints means more learning cycles, more infrastructure built, more returns compounding on each other. The operating model that runs parallel workstreams does not just produce output faster. It compounds faster.

Most companies miss this because they adopt agents the way they adopted every tool before — one at a time, bolted onto the existing workflow. A single agent assistant added to a linear process produces a linear process that is slightly faster in one step. That is not compounding. That is the AI subscription that changes nothing on the P&L.

A Co-Operating Model is designed for parallel from the start. When you map the work against the two columns — human owns, agent executes — you are also mapping what can run simultaneously. Every row in the agent column is a potential parallel workstream. The design question is not "should we add this agent?" It is "what runs at the same time, and who is steering?"

She was steering four workstreams at once. That is the job. Not vaguely elevated. Not abstractly strategic. Four parallel outputs moving simultaneously, one human directing the whole system toward a single standard of quality.

That is the ownership split made visible. The agents are doing exactly what the right column says they should do — drafting, documenting, synthesizing, executing on a defined output. She is doing exactly what the left column says the human should do — directing the work, pricing what's good enough, owning the outcome. What used to be a solo production workflow is now a team she manages. The team just doesn't have business cards.

There is one more thing she brings to that arrangement that the ownership table does not capture: a standard. She knows what good looks like. She knows when the copy is sharp and when it is blunt. She knows which frame of the video holds and which one doesn't. She knows what goes out with Compound's name on it and what stays internal. That knowledge is not in any of the four agent workstreams. It lives in her, and she applies it every time she reviews an output.

The failure mode I see most often is not people who refuse to use agents. It is people who use agents and then accept whatever comes back — because output feels like progress. Getting an agent to produce something is not the same as doing good work. It is a first draft. The human who directs agent work has to know the difference between a draft and a result, and has to be willing to call the draft a draft until the result is actually there.

The standard is not something the agent sets. The human sets it before the work starts and holds it through every review cycle. Without that standard, the output is AI slop with a professional's name on it. With it, the output is the work the human would have done — at the speed and scale only the agent can provide.

We had to design that before we could run it. We had to answer, explicitly, which tasks the agent would own and which she would keep. We had to define the handoffs — what she reviews, what she approves, what goes out without her touching it. That design work is what made the model real. Without it, the tools would have been four separate tabs she opened when she felt like it, and the outcome would have looked exactly like the CEO's headcount report I described at the start of this chapter.

You will do the same design work. Not for her role — for the roles in your company. The chapters that follow give you the structure to do it sprint by sprint, starting from whatever your actual constraints are today.

Chapter 6 proves the same ownership split in a different context — and changes the question from "who do we hire?" to "what does the agent take?"

## The *Equation*.

The best operating systems have a one-line version that carries the whole architecture. EOS does it with *Vision + Traction = Healthy Organization* — the two halves of the model on the left, the outcome on the right, and the equals sign carrying the whole argument that you cannot get the outcome without both halves.

Ours is *Co-Intelligence + Rhythm = Compound.*

<!-- DIAGRAM: The Equation as a typographic/visual treatment — "Co-Intelligence + Rhythm = Compound" with brief labels under each term (system / cadence / outcome); mirrors the EOS equation referenced in the preceding sentence -->
<!-- FORMAT: illustration -->
<!-- PRIORITY: must-have -->

Co-Intelligence is the system half — the Co-Operating Model you just read, the designed structure where human and agent intelligence do their respective work against the same problems. It is the *what*.

Rhythm is the cadence half — running the system on a quarterly beat, sprint by sprint, against your real operational constraints. It is the *how often*. The quarterly beat is the evaluation cadence — the cycle where you assess what the last sprint built and what the next one should target. Sprint duration itself is a design decision and can range from days to a full quarter depending on the work.

Compound is the outcome — used as a verb. Not a vague "maturity," not a generic "scale." Compound, in the precise sense your CFO means it. Each sprint produces a return; the infrastructure built in that sprint reduces the cost of the next sprint; the design improvements made between sprints accelerate every sprint that follows. The company compounds on its AI investment the same way a balance sheet compounds on retained earnings. Slowly at first. And then not slowly.

The Equation does the same work for us that *Vision + Traction* does for an EOS company. You can put it on the wall. You can use it to diagnose what is missing. A company with the model but no rhythm has a slide deck — no work shipped. A company with rhythm but no model has activity — no compounding. Both halves, on the same beat, against real constraints — that produces the outcome.

## What's *next*.

You now have the *what*. The next chapter gives you the *how* — the Framework that runs the Co-Operating Model in practice, the Sequence of six stages that carry a sprint from a validated constraint through Signal, Source, Design, Build, Deliver, and Compound, the Rhythm that runs that Sequence quarter after quarter, and the Sprint as the unit of work where all of it lands. The Framework is the answer to the question every CEO asks next: *fine, on Monday morning, what do we actually do?*
